name: Petersen Graph
definition: The Petersen graph is a 10-vertex, 15-edge, 3-regular graph with unusually rich symmetry and many counterexample properties. It is small enough to draw by hand but structured enough to test deep ideas in graph theory.

defining_equations.explanation: P is the Petersen graph and KG(5,2) is the Kneser graph whose vertices are the 2-element subsets of a 5-element set. Two vertices are joined by an edge exactly when the corresponding subsets are disjoint.
V(P) is the vertex set, E(P) is the edge set, and deg(v) is the degree of a vertex v. These equalities say that the Petersen graph has 10 vertices, 15 edges, and every vertex touches exactly 3 edges.

defining_equations.latex: A_{ij} = 1 \text{ if } i \sim j, \quad A_{ij}=0 \text{ otherwise}
defining_equations.explanation: A_ij is an entry of the adjacency matrix. The notation i sim j means that vertices i and j are adjacent, so the matrix records the full edge structure of the graph.

visuals.description: The standard drawing shows an outer pentagon, an inner star, and five spokes joining corresponding outer and inner vertices. This layout makes the 3-regular structure visible because every vertex has two neighbors in a pentagon or star pattern and one spoke neighbor.

origin_history: The graph is named after Julius Petersen, who introduced it in 1898 while studying regular graphs and factorization questions. It became famous because it is visually simple yet resists several naive expectations about cycles, colorings, and decompositions.
importance:
The Petersen graph is one of the most important small graphs in modern graph theory. It is used as a test object for conjectures because it often provides the smallest or cleanest counterexample to plausible statements about regular graphs.

It is central in discussions of Hamiltonian cycles, edge coloring, snarks, graph minors, and symmetry. Because its automorphism group is large and its construction as a Kneser graph is compact, it also connects combinatorics, algebraic graph theory, and computational graph libraries.

In applied settings, the Petersen graph is useful as a compact benchmark for graph algorithms and graph neural networks. Its high symmetry helps reveal whether a method is detecting genuine structure or only memorizing local patterns.
research_trends:
The Petersen graph continues to appear in research on graph neural network expressivity, especially in tests of whether message passing architectures can distinguish non-isomorphic but locally similar structures.

It is also used in spectral graph theory and algebraic graph theory, where eigenvalues, automorphisms, and graph invariants are studied as compact examples of broader phenomena. In computational graph theory, it remains a standard sanity check for graph generation, coloring, matching, and isomorphism routines.
intuition: The Petersen graph feels like a small puzzle with too much symmetry. It looks orderly, but it blocks simple routes such as Hamiltonian cycles and forces many graph theory definitions to be stated carefully.
minimal_example: One model uses the 2-element subsets of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} as vertices. The vertex {1, 2} is connected to {3, 4}, {3, 5}, and {4, 5}, because those are exactly the 2-element subsets disjoint from {1, 2}.

vertices = list(range(10))
edges = [(0,1),(1,2),(2,3),(3,4),(4,0),(5,7),(7,9),(9,6),(6,8),(8,5),(0,5),(1,6),(2,7),(3,8),(4,9)]
degrees = {v: 0 for v in vertices}
for a, b in edges:
    degrees[a] += 1
    degrees[b] += 1
